title: Trump Pushes AI/Data Center Policy; Anthropic CEO Defends Safety Record Amid China Sales Controversy
body:
Washington — As the United States heads toward a contentious midterm election cycle, the political spotlight is intensifying on the nation’s burgeoning artificial‑intelligence sector. President Donald Trump, in a series of remarks released on Tuesday, outlined a new stance that calls for a “balanced” approach to AI development, emphasizing the need for robust data‑center infrastructure while warning against “over‑regulation” that could stifle innovation. At the same time, Anthropic, a leading AI‑safety firm, defended its record on both safety protocols and its commercial ties to China after critics accused the company of compromising national security for profit. The twin narratives underscore a widening debate over how to manage the rapid ascent of artificial superintelligence, a technology that many lawmakers now view as a strategic priority.

Trump’s comments, delivered during a briefing with senior technology advisers, focused on two main pillars: expanding domestic data‑center capacity and establishing a “clear, consistent framework” for AI oversight. He argued that the United States must invest in high‑performance computing facilities to keep pace with rivals such as China and the European Union, which have recently announced multi‑billion‑dollar AI research funds. “We cannot let bureaucracy choke the engines of progress,” the president said, adding that any regulatory regime should be “lean, targeted, and industry‑friendly.” The remarks echo a broader Republican narrative that positions AI as a catalyst for economic growth, job creation, and national security, while casting Democratic proposals for stricter oversight as potentially harmful to American competitiveness.

Across the aisle, Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El‑Sayed of Michigan introduced a dramatically different vision. In a televised town hall, the candidate called for sweeping governmental control of the AI industry, proposing that the federal government take public ownership of roughly half the sector’s market value. El‑Sayed argued that such a move would prevent monopolistic practices, ensure equitable distribution of AI benefits, and protect citizens from “unchecked corporate power.” While his proposal has drawn sharp criticism from both tech executives and libertarian-leaning lawmakers, it reflects growing anxiety among progressives that AI could exacerbate existing inequalities if left solely in private hands.

Amid the policy tug‑of‑war, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, stepped into the fray to defend the company’s safety record and its commercial engagements with Chinese firms. Anthropic, which positions itself as a “human‑centered” AI developer, has faced scrutiny after reports emerged that it continued to sell its Claude language model to Chinese partners despite heightened geopolitical tensions. Amodei asserted that the company adheres to “the highest international safety standards,” and that all cross‑border transactions are subject to rigorous export‑control reviews. He also highlighted that Anthropic’s safety research has been cited in multiple academic papers and that its models have undergone third‑party audits, aiming to reassure skeptics that profit motives have not eclipsed safety commitments.

The clash over AI policy is not merely rhetorical; it has tangible implications for legislation that could be on the floor as early as next month. Senate committees are slated to hold hearings on AI governance, with bipartisan panels expected to examine topics ranging from data privacy and algorithmic bias to the militarization of AI. Industry leaders warn that a heavy‑handed regulatory approach could push research overseas, while consumer advocates argue that without firm safeguards, the technology could entrench surveillance, deepen misinformation, and widen socioeconomic gaps.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of U.S. AI policy will likely hinge on how policymakers reconcile the dual imperatives of fostering innovation and protecting public interest. If Congress adopts a middle‑ground framework—combining targeted oversight with incentives for domestic data‑center expansion—it could set a precedent for responsible AI development that balances economic ambition with ethical responsibility. Conversely, a polarized approach, either overly permissive or excessively restrictive, risks either ceding strategic advantage to rival nations or stifling the very advances that could drive the next wave of technological progress. The coming months will reveal which path lawmakers choose as the nation grapples with the promise and perils of artificial superintelligence.
